routes.description: Establish that early Christian testimony is sufficiently close to apostolic witnesses and historically trustworthy, then use the reported encounters and witness conduct to reduce the plausibility of legend, sincere mistake, and deliberate fabrication in favor of resurrection.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the documentary sources warrant an early apostolic resurrection claim, the cumulative evidence materially disfavors the principal non-resurrection explanations, and the resulting comparative inference meets the motion's strong-evidence threshold despite the event's low prior probability.

motionBridge.description: Show that the cumulative historical case makes Jesus's resurrection sufficiently better supported than the live alternatives to constitute strong historical evidence.

centralBridges.description: Establish the proximity, attribution, informed access, independence, and general trustworthiness needed for Pauline, Lukan, Johannine, and related testimony to carry historical weight.
Trace resurrection proclamation and encounter reports to the original apostles early enough to constrain a later-legend explanation.
Show that the character of the reported encounters and witness conduct reduces sincere-mistake and deliberate-fabrication explanations, shifting support toward resurrection.
Explain how multiple convergent evidential lines can overcome a low prior probability without treating unusual content alone as disqualifying.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use independently checkable details, undesigned coincidences, and contextual or literary features as defeasible support for source reliability.
Provide case-specific criteria that distinguish the Christian reports from competing religious or extraordinary claims under a consistent evidential method.

routes.description: Establish that the surviving Christian reports are too anonymous, indirect, dependent, textually uncertain, and inaccessible to investigation to support the claimed resurrection, while preserving ordinary error, story development, and deception as live possibilities.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the sources lack adequate independent warrant or testability, the move from reports to bodily resurrection remains underdetermined, or the proposed standard cannot distinguish this claim from comparable rejected claims, leaving the strong-evidence threshold unmet.

motionBridge.description: Show that the surviving reports do not establish resurrection with the strength, testability, and causal connection required by the motion.

centralBridges.description: Demonstrate that anonymity, hearsay, uncertain transmission, dependence, and unavailable examination prevent the reports from functioning like well-grounded eyewitness evidence.
Distinguish the existence or abundance of testimonial claims from independent evidence sufficient to establish the extraordinary event those claims describe.
Preserve legend, shared tradition, sincere error, fabrication, and mixed ordinary explanations without assuming that every narrated encounter occurred as reported.
Require an evidential connection strong enough to overcome the absence of verified comparable resurrections without imposing an a priori prohibition on supernatural events.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether the proposed historical method can accept the Christian reports while principledly rejecting comparable supernatural and religious testimony.
Challenge subsidiary reliability inferences from mundane narrative agreement, vivid detail, embarrassment, martyrdom, and asserted external corroboration.

sections.title: Source Proximity, Attribution, and Testability
sections.rationale: The motion depends first on whether Paul, Acts, the Gospels, and their reported witnesses are sufficiently identifiable, proximate, preserved, and open to verification to ground a strong historical inference.

sections.title: Corroboration, Independence, and Source Reliability
sections.rationale: Claims of undesigned coincidence, ordinary factual accuracy, informed access, and external confirmation must be weighed against shared tradition, literary dependence, textual variation, and the limits of extrapolating from mundane accuracy.

sections.title: Reported Encounters and Competing Explanations
sections.rationale: The central comparative inference turns on whether early proclamation, group and multisensory encounter reports, and witness conduct adequately constrain legend, sincere mistake, deliberate fabrication, or combinations of ordinary causes.

sections.title: Testimonial Standards and Comparative Consistency
sections.rationale: The parties dispute when a claim constitutes evidence, what independent credibility support is required, and whether the same method discriminates consistently among Christian, other religious, and extraordinary reports.

sections.title: Prior Probability, Explanatory Power, and Strong-Evidence Threshold
sections.rationale: Resolution requires connecting the cumulative case or its remaining uncertainties to the motion's demand for strong evidence, including whether low prior probability can be overcome and whether resurrection supplies explanatory power.

moves.speaker: Dr Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: Paul's Corinthian correspondence indicates that resurrection proclamation was already shared with Peter, James, and the original apostolic witnesses.
moves.attributionBasis: The material occurs continuously within McLatchie's timed opening and is framed throughout as his affirmative historical argument.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies an early-apostolic-origin premise through Paul's claimed agreement with Peter, James, and the Twelve.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops an indispensable chronological and apostolic link.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition and named apostolic referents are recoverable, though the evidential limits of reported agreement remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The correspondence supports early shared proclamation, but the claim compresses the warrant from Pauline reporting to independent apostolic confirmation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from Corinthian correspondence to early shared proclamation is coherent, with one bounded source-independence bridge left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific Pauline and apostolic material is identified, but transmission, independence, and the exact content of agreement are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, this directly addresses whether resurrection proclamation reaches the original apostles early.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances its positive historical inference without materially characterizing a competing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly links the Corinthian proclamation with Peter, James, the Twelve, and preaching already known to the Corinthians.

moves.speaker: Dr Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: Acts can report the apostles' early resurrection proclamation with historical weight because its author traveled with Paul, investigated prior testimony, and had access to Jerusalem leaders.
moves.attributionBasis: This is a sustained portion of McLatchie's opening, with explicit transitions identifying Acts, its author, and the proposed reliability inference.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies a source-proximity argument based on companion travel, investigation, and access to Jerusalem witnesses.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops the principal access and reliability bridge for Luke-Acts.

precisionFindings.rationale: The access claim is clear, but phrases such as reliable access and historical weight bundle several distinct reliability propositions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Travel and investigative access are relevant, but they do not alone establish the accuracy of every apostolic report attributed to Acts.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposed access-to-weight inference is valid in defeasible form, though access and investigation do not automatically yield accuracy.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move names concrete access considerations but leaves authorship, dating, and the verification of particular reports materially compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly addresses proximity, informed access, attribution, and source trustworthiness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents affirmative source-access considerations without developing a specific rival account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected material describes Luke-Acts as companion volumes grounded in testimony and links their author to Paul and Jerusalem access.

moves.speaker: Dr Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: The reported appearances were prolonged, collective, and multisensory, making ordinary eyewitness error or hallucination an inadequate explanation of the claimed encounters.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly refers to Dillahunty's prior eyewitness objection and then contrasts it with the reported character of the appearances.

response.rationale: This constructive move argues that the reported encounter characteristics reduce ordinary eyewitness-error and hallucination explanations.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops the comparison with sincere-error alternatives.

precisionFindings.rationale: The encounter characteristics are identifiable, but the move shifts from claimed appearances to their occurrence without an explicit source-reliability condition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Group and multisensory reports may constrain simple error hypotheses, but the move overstates their force without first defending the reports' accuracy.

charity.alternative: Sincere error can concern transmission or interpretation rather than a brief isolated perception.
charity.decisiveQualification: The narrated encounters would constrain only some forms of sincere perceptual error if accurately reported.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative inference is usable, but it leaves a material bridge from narrated encounter properties to historically established properties.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt asserts relevant eyewitness-study conditions but does not substantiate the encounter reports or compare broader sincere-error mechanisms.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly bears on whether honest mistake adequately explains the reported appearances.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly contrasts rapid eyewitness events but narrows sincere error to circumstances unlike the broader live alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts rapid, stranger, or weapon-focused eyewitness conditions with the claimed nature of the resurrection appearances.

moves.speaker: Dr Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: The apostles' reported willingness to suffer and die for their resurrection conviction weighs against their knowingly inventing the claim.
moves.attributionBasis: McLatchie explicitly introduces the deliberate-deception alternative and presents martyrdom and personal transformation as his answer to it.

response.rationale: This constructive move uses reported costly conduct to reduce the likelihood of deliberate apostolic fabrication.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it materially develops the deliberate-deception branch of the alternative comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is recoverable, but the scope of which apostles suffered or died for which avoidable affirmation is not fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker properly distinguishes sincere martyrdom from dying for a known lie, but the historical and causal premises remain underdocumented.

charity.alternative: People may suffer for sincere but mistaken beliefs rather than for claims they knowingly fabricated.
charity.decisiveQualification: Costly conduct bears specifically against knowing invention, not against sincere mistake or later legendary development.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is coherent when limited to knowing fabrication, and the speaker expressly avoids treating suffering as proof of truth.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Reported willingness to suffer is relevant, but the move provides limited representative support for deaths tied to recantable eyewitness claims.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly attacks deliberate fabrication as one principal non-resurrection explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move explicitly preserves sincere belief as a live explanation and limits its inference to known deception.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that apostles were willing to suffer and die while explicitly distinguishing sincere conviction from dying for a known lie.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: The biblical reports are anonymous, altered, unexamined accounts without identifiable witnesses or corroborating physical evidence, so they cannot establish a resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: The argument follows directly in Dillahunty's uninterrupted opening and applies his previously stated evidential standard specifically to the biblical material.

components.text: Whether Luke-Acts has identifiable, informed, and historically testable access to apostolic witnesses.
Whether Pauline material independently establishes the original apostles' resurrection proclamation.
Whether the narrated encounter characteristics may be treated as established historical observations.

response.rationale: The reply directly contests source identification, examination, alteration, and corroboration, contacting the access premise while also challenging reliance on narrated appearances.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts decisive source and verification premises but does not separately analyze every proposed Pauline and Lukan link.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection is clear, but anonymous, altered, propaganda, and biblical reports are used broadly without source-by-source qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The absence of oath or cross-examination weakens testability, but saying the material cannot establish resurrection imposes a stronger threshold than defended here.

charity.alternative: Ancient reports can have historical weight without oath, cross-examination, or surviving named depositions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Their weight still depends on attribution, transmission, independence, and corroboration that can be assessed by historical methods.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The source-limitations inference is coherent, though the move partly conflates reduced testability with categorical inability to establish the event.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It identifies concrete deficiencies, but applies anonymity and alteration broadly without a differentiated account of Paul, Acts, and individual traditions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, the reply directly attacks attribution, transmission, examination, and corroborative access.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply identifies genuine limitations but treats forensic safeguards as closer to necessary conditions than the pro case claimed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls the material anonymous and altered, notes the absence of oath or questioning, and stresses known eyewitness unreliability.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Treating anonymous ancient testimonial material as strong evidence would admit comparably weak supernatural and fraudulent claims under the same standard.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker remains Matt throughout this continuous standards-of-evidence argument, with the moderator transition occurring only after the subsequent concluding move.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies a consistency test requiring the testimonial standard to avoid admitting comparably weak extraordinary claims.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly establishes the cross-claim discrimination demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative demand is clear, though strong evidence shifts between physical documentation and examined, bias-screened testimony.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Consistency is necessary, but the specified courtroom-like safeguards are presented with insufficient defense as requirements for historical evidence.

charity.alternative: Ancient historical claims may be assessed by source criticism even when cross-examination and physical evidence are unavailable.
charity.decisiveQualification: The same relaxed historical criteria must still discriminate among analogous extraordinary claims consistently.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The symmetry challenge is strong, but the move leaves a material bridge from lack of forensic safeguards to equivalence with fraudulent claims.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It identifies relevant testimonial safeguards but supplies no representative competing claim or detailed demonstration of evidential parity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: At the top of the subsidiary tier, it directly establishes a demanding cross-claim consistency test.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move preserves the legitimate consistency demand, though it understates non-forensic methods of evaluating ancient testimony.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines strong evidence through documentation, questioning, reporting, and bias checks, then compares the biblical material with weaker claims.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: The pro case begins by assuming events needing explanation while overlooking legend as an explanation of the resurrection story itself.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt explicitly characterizes Jonathan's explanatory framework and closes his opening statement immediately after presenting the legend objection.

components.text: Whether narrated appearance properties can be assumed before explaining how the resurrection story developed.
Whether the alternatives may be restricted to explanations accepting the reported events substantially as narrated.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses the pro framework as beginning too far downstream: legend may explain the reports themselves, so narrated events cannot simply define the explanatory data.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly identifies the disputed assumption and states why that assumption distorts the alternative comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between explaining narrated events and explaining the story is explicit, stable, and adequately bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move advances legend as an overlooked live possibility rather than claiming to have established a complete legendary explanation.

charity.alternative: The pro case may treat early reports, rather than every narrative detail, as data requiring explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: It must independently warrant which reported events are historical before using their narrated character against legend.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The diagnosis cleanly distinguishes story-level and event-level explanation and states the consequence for the pro alternative set.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual objection is strong, though the move offers little positive evidence about the actual process or timing of legendary development.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly preserves legend by challenging the assumed historical data used to exclude it.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the pro case's explanatory aim while identifying the decisive qualification concerning what counts as established data.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says the pro case assumes a person, death, and resurrection account needing explanation and begins too far down the track.

moves.speaker: Dr Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: A miracle's low prior probability warrants greater scrutiny but can still be overcome by a sufficiently powerful cumulative documentary case.
moves.attributionBasis: Jonathan concedes Matt's demand for greater scrutiny and develops a sustained probability argument and analogy before transitioning to a separate challenge about acceptable evidence.

components.text: Whether a low-prior extraordinary claim can ever be supported strongly enough by cumulative documentary evidence.
Whether documentary evidence lacking direct present examination is categorically incapable of overcoming a low prior.

response.rationale: The reply accepts heightened scrutiny and directly argues that multiple evidential lines may overcome a low prior, although its analogy does not validate the actual resurrection evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive in-principle prior question but does not satisfy the source-specific verification demands.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition distinguishes greater scrutiny from categorical exclusion and expressly conditions success on sufficiently powerful cumulative evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move makes the appropriately limited claim that a low prior can be overcome, not that this case has already overcome it.

charity.alternative: Low prior probability requires unusually strong likelihood evidence rather than making the claim impossible.
charity.decisiveQualification: The actual documentary lines must be independently warranted and much more expected on resurrection than on alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The lottery analogy validly illustrates the general Bayesian point that sufficiently discriminating evidence can overcome a low prior.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The analogy supports the in-principle claim but does not show that the debated sources possess comparable independence or discriminating power.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly supplies the route's required explanation of how cumulative evidence could overcome a low prior.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response accurately accepts enhanced scrutiny and addresses the strongest non-exclusionary version of the prior objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt uses convergent documentary signs of a lottery win to illustrate how multiple evidence items can outweigh a very low prior.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Legend and sincere error remain live alternatives because ancient reports alone do not justify assuming the narrated events occurred as described.
moves.attributionBasis: After the moderator assigns Matt the floor, Matt directly revisits Jonathan's four alternatives and sustains this response until turning to a distinct explanatory-likelihood objection.

components.text: Whether claimed encounter details may be assumed historical when evaluating legend and sincere error.
Whether the pro alternative set improperly presupposes the substantial accuracy of the narratives.
Whether cumulative evidence overcomes alternatives when its component reports remain insufficiently warranted.

response.rationale: The reply directly rejects beginning inside the story and preserves legend and sincere error, but it does not develop their mechanisms or comparative likelihoods in detail.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive assumption behind the alternative comparison but leaves the positive rival explanations underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes assuming narrated events from assessing whether reports justify that assumption.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Legend and sincere error are preserved as live possibilities without being asserted as conclusively established explanations.

charity.alternative: The pro case may rely on a historically filtered core rather than assuming every narrative element.
charity.decisiveQualification: The filtering method still must independently establish which core events occurred before using them against rivals.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reply coherently preserves alternatives by challenging the evidential status of the narrated facts on which their exclusion depends.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The source-status critique is material, but the move offers limited affirmative evidence for particular legend or sincere-error pathways.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly preserves two principal ordinary alternatives against the pro comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response recognizes the explanatory framework but fairly disputes its starting data rather than caricaturing every pro premise.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says legend concerns how the story arises and rejects assuming that the reported events happened before comparing explanations.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Paul, Luke, and John do not provide strong resurrection evidence because their relevant claims are indirect, unverifiable, or anonymously transmitted.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt introduces Jonathan's maximal-data case and then examines its principal Pauline, Lukan, and Johannine sources continuously before shifting to an overall recap.

components.text: Whether Luke-Acts supplies sufficiently direct, attributable, and verifiable access to resurrection witnesses.
Whether Paul's indirect position can nevertheless establish early apostolic resurrection proclamation.
Whether the cumulative case has adequately warranted the sources composing it.

response.rationale: The reply directly examines the Pauline, Lukan, and Johannine source chain, but it sometimes treats lack of direct eyewitness status as more dispositive than the pro argument requires.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the central proximity and verification components while incompletely addressing indirect corroborative arguments.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source-chain objection is recoverable, but the broad claim that Paul is not a witness blurs his claimed experience and his access to earlier apostles.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Indirectness and anonymity materially weaken the case, but the suggestion that Paul's statements cannot be strong evidence is insufficiently qualified.

charity.alternative: Paul need not witness Jesus's ministry to transmit early claims from Peter, James, and other apostles.
charity.decisiveQualification: His testimony still requires a warranted chain from those contacts to the particular resurrection propositions asserted.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The source-chain critique is coherent, though it occasionally moves too quickly from non-eyewitness status to evidential incapacity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It identifies concrete limitations in Paul, Luke, and John but does not fully engage evidence offered for informed access and early contact.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly attacks the proximity, attribution, and verification of the case's principal sources.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply reaches the indirectness problem but understates the evidential value that informed secondary testimony could possess.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies Paul as not witnessing Jesus's life, death, or resurrection and places that objection within a broader review of Luke and John.

moves.speaker: Dr Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: Numerous subtle interconnections and external confirmations cumulatively indicate that the Gospel and Acts authors were close to the facts and had substantially reliable access to information.
moves.attributionBasis: McLatchie introduces the move as an inductive cumulative argument and supplies an extended undesigned-coincidence example comparing chronological details in John and Mark.

components.text: Whether internal interconnections and external confirmations can support reliable source access despite disputed authorship.
Whether anonymous or unexamined sources can acquire historical weight through independently checkable features.

response.rationale: The reply addresses reliability through cumulative confirmations and an undesigned-coincidence example, but it does not fully answer attribution, dependence, or resurrection-specific verification.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the source-reliability challenge while leaving several decisive source-chain limitations unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative proposition is clear, but numerous confirmations, close to facts, and substantially trustworthy remain broad and unevenly scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A subtle chronology fit can support some access, but it does not without further comparison establish broad substantial trustworthiness.

charity.alternative: Shared knowledge, literary dependence, or ordinary contextual accuracy can produce interconnections without independent eyewitness access.
charity.decisiveQualification: An undesigned coincidence carries greater weight only if dependence and common-source explanations are comparatively disfavored.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inductive form is coherent, but the generalization from selected interconnections to substantial overall trustworthiness leaves a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A concrete John-Mark example is supplied, yet representativeness, independence, external confirmations, and rival mechanisms remain underdefended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: At the top of the subsidiary tier, it directly advances corroborative source features and reliability indicators.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move mentions cumulative induction but labels competing dependence explanations inadequate without sustained comparative treatment.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt claims numerous historical confirmations and introduces undesigned coincidences as cumulative evidence of close factual access.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Agreement on ordinary Passover-era details can arise from shared circulating stories and does not establish either source independence or the truth of a resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty questions the unspecified dating and independence assumptions, then contrasts agreement on mundane narrative details with the supernatural conclusion under debate.

components.text: Whether mundane narrative agreement establishes independence, general trustworthiness, or resurrection-specific accuracy.

response.rationale: The reply directly contacts the inference from ordinary interconnection to broad reliability, offering shared documents and circulating stories as alternative explanations.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly addresses both the claimed corroborative feature and the inferential gap to resurrection.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reply clearly separates ordinary agreement, source independence, and the supernatural conclusion without material ambiguity.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that mundane agreement does not by itself establish resurrection or independence is well matched to the offered support.

charity.alternative: Mundane interconnections may defeasibly increase confidence in a source's access even if they do not directly prove resurrection.
charity.decisiveQualification: That increase must account for dependence and cannot be transferred automatically to extraordinary claims.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reply cleanly distinguishes corroboration of ordinary setting from proof of independence and from warrant for the resurrection conclusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It supplies plausible shared-source mechanisms and a concrete Passover example, with only a bounded gap in documenting actual dependence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: At the top of the subsidiary tier, it directly attacks extrapolation from mundane narrative features to resurrection reliability.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants ordinary agreement while accurately limits what it can establish about independence and resurrection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites Markan copying and shared stories, then argues that agreement about Jesus being in town near Passover does not establish resurrection.

moves.speaker: Dr Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: Shared oral tradition does not defeat undesigned coincidences across distinct narrative units and may itself preserve rather than explain away an evidential interconnection.
moves.attributionBasis: McLatchie recognizes the oral-source objection, references prior engagement with it, and gives several reasons he believes it fails to explain the interconnections.

components.text: Whether shared oral tradition adequately explains interconnections across distinct narrative units.
Whether derivative oral material necessarily defeats the reliability inference from narrative interlocking.

response.rationale: The reply directly argues that oral derivation may preserve an undesigned connection, but its ad-hocness charge does not independently compare common-source and truth hypotheses.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the shared-tradition mechanism but incompletely addresses the resurrection-specific extrapolation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The principal claim is recoverable, but distinct narrative units and undesigned coincidence are not specified enough to secure independence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Showing compatibility with oral tradition does not make truth the simplest explanation, and the ad-hocness conclusion exceeds the supplied comparison.

charity.alternative: Shared oral traditions can preserve coordinated details across texts without independent access by each author.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such a hypothesis requires evidence of common transmission but is not ad hoc merely because it competes with source truth.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The point that oral transmission need not erase an evidential connection is coherent, but compatibility is treated as comparative explanation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move asserts distinct pericopes and simplicity but supplies insufficient evidence against shared-source transmission or literary dependence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly defends corroborative interconnections against a shared-oral-tradition challenge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the oral-tradition alternative but dismisses it as ad hoc without addressing its strongest dependence rationale.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that even derivation from earlier oral traditions could retain an undesigned coincidence and calls the rival explanation ad hoc.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Reliance on preferred Christian reports supplies no principled epistemic distinction between those reports and rejected supernatural claims from other religions.
moves.attributionBasis: The wording continues Dillahunty's direct challenge to McLatchie and is followed by McLatchie's explicit defense of New Testament sources.

components.text: Whether the pro reliability criteria distinguish Christian sources from rejected religious reports.
Whether cumulative evidence is applied consistently across religious claims.
Whether preference for truth over shared tradition reflects a principled evidential rule.

response.rationale: The reply directly demands a discriminating epistemic criterion and alleges selective acceptance, though it does not present a detailed comparator with matched evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive consistency demand but does not substantiate equivalence between particular competing cases.

precisionFindings.rationale: The demand for a principled distinction is clear, but other religions and their claims remain unspecified and potentially heterogeneous.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A consistent method is necessary, but the claim that no distinction was given is broader than the excerpt's limited comparative showing warrants.

charity.alternative: Christian reports may differ in proximity, multiplicity, corroboration, or fit with background evidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those differences must be demonstrated rather than assumed and applied by criteria usable across cases.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The consistency challenge is coherent and identifies the consequence of accepting preferred reports without a cross-applicable evidential rule.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move establishes a methodological demand but provides little evidence that relevant competing religious cases are actually evidentially comparable.

relevanceBurden.rationale: At the top of the subsidiary tier, it directly advances cross-claim consistency and discrimination requirements.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply allows that a distinction could exist and properly asks how evidence would establish it, though comparators are underspecified.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks how accepted Christian accounts differ epistemically from other rejected religious claims and alleges that no differentiating method was supplied.

moves.speaker: Dr Jonathan McLatchie
moves.proposition: Extraordinary testimony should be assessed case by case for witness trustworthiness, deception, honest error, and prior probability rather than rejected solely because of unusual content.
moves.attributionBasis: The response follows Dillahunty's challenge to McLatchie, states McLatchie's recurring hypothesis-testing framework, and introduces his alien-travel prior-probability comparison.

components.text: Whether extraordinary religious reports should be distinguished through case-specific, consistently applied reliability criteria.
Whether extraordinary testimony must satisfy a uniform evidential standard rather than be rejected for unusual content.
Whether witness access, deception, and error should be evaluated source by source.

response.rationale: The reply justifies replacing a category-level religious comparison with case-specific tests of trustworthiness, deception, error, and prior probability, preserving the consistency issue.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within justified reframes, it states the replacement criteria and retains the legitimate demand for evidential discrimination.

precisionFindings.rationale: The case-specific framework and its principal criteria are explicit, stable, and appropriately conditional.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that these factors must be assessed is methodological and proportionate; it does not assert that the Christian case passes them.

charity.alternative: A consistent cross-religious standard requires comparable scrutiny rather than rejection by religious category.
charity.decisiveQualification: Case-specific analysis satisfies consistency only if the same criteria and evidential thresholds are genuinely applied across cases.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The framework coherently separates unusual content from source trustworthiness, deception, sincere error, and prior probability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The methodological criteria are well motivated, though this span does not demonstrate that the debated witnesses satisfy them.

relevanceBurden.rationale: At the top of the subsidiary tier, it directly supplies case-specific criteria for cross-claim discrimination.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the strongest consistency concern and supplies a legitimate, content-neutral replacement method.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt lists witness trustworthiness, likelihood of lying, honest mistake, dreams, and prior probability as case-specific assessment factors.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: A natural alien-visitation hypothesis need not be less probable than a resurrection that violates known natural regularities, especially when no comparable resurrection has been scientifically verified.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly disputes McLatchie's alien prior-probability claim and frames the contrast using Dillahunty's naturalistic evidential standard before asking for verified cases.

components.text: How the prior probability of resurrection compares with natural extraordinary hypotheses under case-specific assessment.
Whether the absence of verified comparable resurrections creates an especially demanding evidential threshold.

response.rationale: The reply directly contests the proposed prior comparison and invokes the absence of scientifically verified resurrections, though it does not quantify priors or likelihoods.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive prior-probability question but does not answer the full cumulative-evidence argument.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative-prior point is recoverable, but scientifically verified and natural regularities are not operationally specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The absence of verified cases supports a low prior, but it does not alone determine comparison with every alien-visitation hypothesis.

charity.alternative: A singular event can have a very low prior yet be established by evidence with a sufficiently large likelihood ratio.
charity.decisiveQualification: The lack of comparable verified resurrections raises the evidential burden without creating an a priori exclusion.
